newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Hurricane Lili passes Bermuda, Bahamas clean up.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Lili passes Bermuda, Bahamas clean up.

text.p: Crews worked to restore power to the battered islands of the central Bahamas on Sunday as Hurricane Lili raced through the Atlantic, sparing Bermuda the worst of its 90 mph (145 kph) winds.

Heavy rain pelted the British colony in the north Atlantic but the center of the storm remained far enough offshore that authorities did not consider it a threat and did not gear up its emergency center or advise residents to batten down.

At 11 a.m. EDT (1500 GMT), the center of Lili was located at latitude 30.0 north, longitude 64.2 west, about 155 miles (250 km) south of Bermuda, and moving northeast at 25 mph (41 kph), the U.S. National Hurricane Center said in Miami.
Its maximum winds had decreased and additional weakening was expected in the next 24 hours, forecasters said.

Lili appeared to be fading after a damaging rampage that began last week off the coast of Central America. Flooding from the storm was blamed for 10 deaths in Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica before it moved north over Cuba and then east through the central Bahamas.

Bahamas government officials on Sunday toured the hard-hit islands of San Salvador, Great Exuma and Long Island, where Lili ripped roofs off dozens of homes, flooded streets and damaged banana crops, the Bahamas Broadcasting Corp. reported.
No casualties were reported, but electricity to many parts of the islands was cut and emergency crews were working to repair toppled poles and shredded lines.

Officials said few houses had been spared damage from the storm in San Salvador, a 25-mile long (40 km) island which claims to be the first place in the New World where explorer Christopher Columbus set foot in 1492.
Cuban authorities reported no deaths from the storm but said it had damaged or destroyed 29,000 homes and caused widespread damage to crops including sugar cane, citrus fruits and bananas.
The central province of Cienfuegos was the worst hit, with about 2,000 homes destroyed and damage to crops including vegetables and coffee.
